title: 基于自适应的强化学习的动态奖励函数优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for reinforcement learning, leveraging adaptive reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust reward functions in response to changing input data. Traditional reinforcement learning models often rely on static reward functions, limiting their ability to adapt to dynamic environments. We introduce a dynamic reward function optimization technique that iteratively updates the reward function based on the observed data, enhancing learning stability and performance. The core mechanism involves employing a self-adaptive reinforcement learning algorithm to continuously refine the reward function, providing a more robust and responsive learning process. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in convergence speed and overall performance compared to baseline methods.

title: Quantum Entanglement Non-Linear Computation: An Adaptive Algorithm
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, offers unprecedented computational capabilities. This paper explores the design and implementation of a novel quantum computation algorithm, termed "Quantum Entanglement Non-Linear Computation" (QENLC), which leverages dynamically adjusted quantum state configurations to achieve enhanced parallelism and complex operations. The core mechanism centers on a "Quantum Entanglement Self-Adaptation" (QEAS) process, which iteratively adjusts the entanglement strength and direction based on real-time quantum state evolution. We demonstrate the algorithm's potential to surpass classical computational limitations by exploiting the inherent dynamism of quantum systems. This work presents a framework for dynamically shaping quantum states, offering a pathway to significantly accelerate computations and enable new quantum algorithms.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Neural Network Representation
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Topology for Neural Network Representation (ATNR) method designed to dynamically adjust the topology of neural network representations during training. Traditional approaches often treat topology as fixed, limiting the model's ability to adapt to the data. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging a neural network to learn a 'map' of the network's internal structure, which is continuously updated as the training proceeds. The core mechanism is a continuous updating of this map, allowing the network to adapt to the data's specific characteristics, ultimately improving generalization and efficiency. We present a framework for training ATNR, detailing the neural network architecture, training procedure, and evaluation results demonstrating its effectiveness. The study explores the impact of different network architectures and training strategies on the performance of ATNR.

title: An Agent Model Abstraction for Human-AI Teaming Cognitive Coupling
abstract: Industrial environments increasingly rely on collaboration between humans and AI-enabled agents. Effective teamwork requires aligning how agents perceive situations, plan actions to pursue goals, and adapt to changing conditions, yet existing systems lack mechanisms for cross-agent cognitive processes coupling. This paper presents a conceptual cognitive agent model that formalises cognitive coupling through eight components: Input, Process, Output, State, Value, Memory, World Model, and Goal. The model abstracts how agents coordinate and co-regulate their cognitive cycles, providing a basis for analysing distributed cognition and designing cognitively interoperable human-AI systems.

title: Adapting from Downturns: Prediction of Long-Term Conversational-Skill Development in Mental-Health Crisis Counselors
abstract: How do people learn to become better conversationalists? This question is especially important in the context of mental-health counseling, where conversational skills are essential, yet volunteer counselors often have limited access to supervision and structured feedback. Understanding how counselors develop their ability to steer conversations toward positive outcomes -- and identifying early which counselors are (not) on track to improve -- can help prioritize support for the counselors who need it most. In this work, we introduce the task of predicting, early in a conversationalist's career, whether they will eventually improve at steering conversations toward positive outcomes, and demonstrate the feasibility of this task in the case of volunteer mental-health crisis counselors. Our central insight is that people may struggle with particular kinds of moments in a conversation, and that what is especially revealing of their likelihood of future improvement is how they learn to handle those moments over time. We operationalize this insight by designing a method that identifies the types of moments a counselor initially struggles with, captures how they adapt their response when they re-encounter similar moments in subsequent conversations, and learns which early adaptations predict improvement months or even years later. While this future-prediction task is challenging, our counselor-adaptation approach yields better results than baselines that learn directly from the conversation transcript.

title: Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection
abstract: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

title: String problems in the congested clique model
abstract: In this paper we present algorithms for several string problems in the Congested Clique model. In the Congested Clique model, n nodes (computers) are used to solve some problem. The input to the problem is distributed among the nodes, and the communication between the nodes is conducted in rounds. In each round, every node is allowed to send an $$O(\log n)$$ -bit message to every other node in the network. We consider three fundamental string problems in the Congested Clique model. First, we present an O(1)-round algorithm for string sorting. Second, we present an O(1)-round combinatorial pattern matching algorithm. Finally, we present an $$O(\log \log n)$$ -round algorithm for the computation of the Suffix Array and the corresponding Longest Common Prefix array of a given string. To obtain these algorithms, we develop a sorting procedure for large keys of polynomial size, extending the prior sorting algorithm of Lenzen [PODC’13], which handles only $$O(\log n)$$ -bit keys. This new procedure may be of independent interest.

title: Lost in Reordering: Structural Sensitivity of Multilingual LLMs under Semantics-Preserving Perturbations
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate strong multilingual reasoning performance, yet their robustness to semantics-preserving structural variation remains underexplored, particularly for relatively free word-order languages. We investigate the structural sensitivity of multilingual LLMs using two linguistically grounded perturbation settings in Hindi and Malayalam: constrained constituent reordering and active-passive voice transformation. We introduce a benchmark dataset IndicReStruct, with two variants, GSM8K-Reordered and GSM8K-Voice, constructed from GSM8K while preserving semantic meaning. Across six state-of-the-art LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, we observe consistent and significant degradation in mathematical reasoning performance under structurally perturbed inputs. To further understand these failures, we perform qualitative error analysis and mechanistic interpretability experiments using residual-stream activation patching. Our analyses show that reasoning failures frequently arise from disruptions in entity-quantity alignment and that intermediate transformer layers contribute most strongly toward reasoning restoration. Overall, our findings suggest that current multilingual LLMs remain highly sensitive to surface syntactic realization and lack robust compositional invariance under structurally different but semantically equivalent inputs.

title: The Head Complexity of Boolean Functions in Single-Layer Attention
abstract: What can a single layer of self-attention compute? We study head complexity: the minimum number of attention heads required to compute a function in a one-layer attention-only model. We establish an exact hierarchy under this measure: $k$ heads compute $k$-bit parity but cannot compute $(k+1)$-bit parity. The lower bound is unconditional in the two resources a transformer might otherwise exploit; it holds at unbounded embedding dimension and unbounded numerical precision. The proof rests on an alternating-sum obstruction: after clearing the softmax denominators, every monomial in the resulting decision polynomial omits at least one of the $k+1$ input bits, forcing its correlation with parity to vanish. The same obstruction yields lower bounds for related tasks, including the well-studied multi-hop induction-head task. We also establish compactness bounds for embedding dimension and numerical precision. Specifically, a compactness theorem shows that any function computable at all can be computed with embedding dimension and precision bounded by the discrete data of the task, namely, head count, alphabet size, and length. Thus, potentially unbounded dimension or precision provably cannot substitute for heads. Finally, we derive nearly matching universal bounds for general binary functions: $2^n$ heads suffice to compute every $n$-bit binary function, with one head per monomial in its multilinear expansion, while a counting argument shows almost all such functions require $Ω(2^n/n^2)$ heads. This lower bound matches the upper bound to within a $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ factor, even when dimension and precision are unbounded. Together, these results characterize head requirements for Boolean computation in this model.

abstract: Vi har brug for mindre AI for at nå næste trin på AI-modenhedstrappen. For at blive bedre med AI bliver vi simpelthen nødt til at bruge det mindre. title: Quantum-Based Geometric Simulation for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: Quantum-based geometric simulation offers a promising approach to handling high-dimensional data, leveraging the unique properties of quantum mechanics to represent and analyze complex patterns. This paper proposes a novel quantum algorithm for simulating high-dimensional data, centered around the concept of quantum superposition to explore the data's inherent structure, aiming to achieve a more accurate representation than traditional geometric methods. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum superposition to identify and quantify relationships within the data, potentially uncovering hidden structures and trends that are difficult to discern with classical approaches. The paper details the algorithm's design, its theoretical underpinnings, and initial experimental validation, showcasing the potential for enhanced data analysis and representation.

title: Dynamic Information Entropy: A Novel Algorithm for Pattern and Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic information entropy calculation and application method. Traditional entropy calculation methods are static, failing to adapt effectively to data variations. We propose a dynamic algorithm that adjusts entropy values based on data input shifts, enabling more robust pattern and anomaly detection. The core mechanism involves a combination of dynamic entropy calculation with machine learning models, which analyzes input changes to dynamically adjust entropy. This approach offers improved adaptability and detection capabilities compared to static methods. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to identify subtle patterns and anomalies in diverse datasets. We conclude with a discussion of the potential applications of this dynamic entropy calculation method across various fields, including data mining, security analysis, and anomaly detection in industrial processes.

title: Quantum Information Modulation: Adaptive Geometry Optimization
abstract: Quantum Information Modulation (QIM) offers a promising approach to enhance quantum computation through dynamic adjustment of quantum states. This paper investigates the application of QIM to optimize quantum information processing, specifically focusing on achieving more efficient quantum communication. We introduce a novel self-adaptive geometric optimization strategy, leveraging the inherent properties of quantum information modulation to dynamically adjust qubit states and improve the performance of quantum algorithms. This system demonstrates the potential for significant advancements in quantum communication and computation. The core mechanism involves the controlled evolution of quantum states through instantaneous shifts, allowing for optimized performance in complex scenarios. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional optimization techniques, offering a pathway towards more robust and efficient quantum systems.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Contrastive Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection in graph data leveraging the principles of contrastive learning. Traditional graph anomaly detection methods often struggle with capturing complex graph structures and subtle deviations. Our method learns robust graph embeddings by training a contrastive network to maximize similarity between nodes belonging to the same community and minimize similarity between nodes from different communities. This effectively encodes the normal graph structure, allowing anomalies – characterized by unusual node relationships – to be identified as significant deviations from learned embeddings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline a framework adaptable to various graph datasets. The core of the method lies in learning representations that inherently distinguish normal behavior from anomalous behavior. The proposed technique offers a potentially significant improvement over existing anomaly detection techniques for graph data.

title: The title is: A Unified Memory-Centric Computing Architecture: Version 2.0 — Lie-Computable, OTOC-Scheduled Reconfigurable Systems
abstract: Here is the abstract from the uploaded paper, preserving its framing and terminology: Abstract Reconfigurable computing has traditionally relied on classical field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), in which computation emerges from memory through lookup tables and routing. In prior work, we introduced a unified memory-based architecture extending this paradigm to quantum and DNA-based memory substrates. In this paper, we present Version 2.0 of this architecture by introducing a mathematically rigorous scheduling and computability framework based on lattice Lie computability and out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs). We show that computation on quantum, spintronic, and genomic memory fabrics is governed not by time-ordered execution but by operator growth, non-commutativity, and Lie algebra closure. OTOCs provide a physically measurable norm that bounds operator scrambling and enables non-time-ordered, coherence-preserving reconfiguration. This establishes a unified architecture in which memory, routing, computation, and scheduling are all manifestations of operator algebra dynamics, yielding a principled foundation for scalable hypercomputing across classical, quantum, and synthetic genomic substrates.Source:

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Temporal Logic and Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to reasoning about temporal relationships by integrating temporal logic with neural networks. The core idea is to train a neural network to understand and apply the rules of temporal logic, thereby enabling it to reason more robustly and reliably about events and their temporal dependencies. We propose a mechanism where the neural network learns both the syntax and semantics of temporal logic expressions. This allows the system to effectively represent and manipulate temporal constraints, ultimately leading to improved reasoning performance compared to purely neural or purely symbolic approaches. The work highlights the potential for creating hybrid systems that leverage the strengths of both formal logic and deep learning, offering a path toward more explainable and trustworthy AI systems for temporal reasoning tasks. The key contribution lies in the formalization of temporal reasoning within a neural network framework, providing a structured method for encoding temporal relationships.

title: Non-Linear Quantum Simulation of Quantum Field Theory
abstract: This paper explores the application of a novel quantum simulation technique – a non-linear quantum simulation of quantum field theory – to address limitations in classical calculations of complex quantum systems. We propose a modified Feynman path integral method, enhanced with non-linear interactions, to provide a more accurate and efficient representation of particle interactions and quantum field behavior. This work aims to significantly advance the field of quantum field theory by extending its computational capabilities. The core claim is that this approach offers a potentially faster and more accurate method for simulating complex quantum systems than existing classical techniques. The mechanism involves a quantum version of the Feynman path integral method, incorporating non-linear interactions to achieve improved results. This research is driven by the inherent computational cost limitations of traditional methods and the desire to unlock more accurate representations of quantum phenomena.

title: Neural Topology Dynamic Learning (NTDL)
abstract: This paper introduces Neural Topology Dynamic Learning (NTDL), a novel approach to optimizing deep learning models that leverages the principles of physical topology within neural networks. The core claim of NTDL is that by simulating the dynamic changes in physical topological connections mimicking biological neural networks, we can significantly enhance the generalization ability and robustness of deep learning models. Unlike traditional methods focused on individual neuron weight adjustments, NTDL directly manipulates the network's topology, learning to 'break' weak connections and 'build' new ones based on model performance and simulated perturbations. We utilize information geometry and topological data analysis to quantify and guide these topological changes. The proposed framework offers a fundamentally different perspective on model optimization, drawing parallels with the intricate dynamics of synaptic plasticity in biological neural networks and introducing a topological analytical framework to direct the optimization process. Experimental validation (not presented in this document) is anticipated to demonstrate the effectiveness of NTDL in improving model performance across a range of tasks. ---

title: Fractal Neural Networks for Complex Data Analysis
abstract: This paper introduces Fractal Neural Networks (FNNs), a novel approach to complex data analysis leveraging the principles of fractal geometry. Traditional neural networks often falter when dealing with data exhibiting self-similar patterns and intricate structures, primarily due to their limitations in capturing hierarchical and recursive relationships. FNNs overcome these challenges by constructing networks with recursive connections and self-similar modules, mimicking the inherent patterns found in natural and complex datasets. The core idea is to build networks where smaller units recursively generate larger structures, mirroring fractal characteristics. This allows for a more efficient representation and processing of data with complex dependencies. The architecture is designed to detect and exploit these self-similarities, leading to improved accuracy and robustness in analyzing complex data. This work presents the foundational design and theoretical underpinnings of FNNs, outlining their key components and potential applications.

The core idea is to build networks where smaller units recursively generate larger structures, mirroring fractal characteristics. This allows for a more efficient representation and processing of data with complex dependencies. The architecture is designed to detect and exploit these self-similarities, leading to improved accuracy and robustness in analyzing complex data. This work presents the foundational design and theoretical underpinnings of FNNs, outlining their key components and potential applications.

title: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Adaptive Control of Complex Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum reservoir computing (QRC) for adaptive control of complex dynamical systems. The core concept leverages quantum superposition and entanglement within a reservoir of coupled qubits to enhance the accuracy and speed of control signal generation. Unlike traditional reservoir computing, this approach explicitly utilizes quantum phenomena for improved performance. A small, randomly coupled quantum system, acting as the reservoir, is exposed to the dynamics of the system being controlled. The output of the reservoir is then used to train a classical controller, capitalizing on quantum interference effects. We present a theoretical framework outlining the methodology and demonstrate, through mathematical analysis, the potential advantages of QRC over conventional control methods, particularly for highly nonlinear systems. The work explores the key parameters influencing QRC performance, including the number of qubits, coupling strengths, and the training algorithm. Initial results suggest a significant improvement in control accuracy and convergence speed compared to classical reservoir approaches.

title: Hierarchical Modular Logic for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction is a fundamental requirement for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. Current error correction schemes face significant limitations in scalability and complexity. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical modular logic system designed to address these challenges by introducing a layered approach to quantum state encoding and decoding. This system leverages a progressive encoding and decoding process, improving resilience against propagation errors and enabling the construction of more complex quantum algorithms. We detail the design of this modular architecture, exploring its potential impact on error correction capabilities and the underlying mathematical principles guiding its implementation. The paper concludes with a discussion of the advantages and challenges of this approach, outlining future research directions.

title: Multi-Agent Learning for Robot Collaborative Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Multi-Agent Learning (MAL) to robot collaborative optimization. The core claim is that MAL can effectively facilitate coordination between robots, enabling solutions to complex environmental adaptation and task execution challenges. The proposed approach constructs a reinforcement learning-based multi-agent learning model and analyzes the interaction strategies between individual agents. The novelty lies in leveraging MAL to enhance collaboration and adaptability within a robot system, addressing limitations of traditional centralized control methods. This research explores the fundamental principles of MAL and its potential for robust, scalable robotic solutions. The paper presents a theoretical framework and discusses key considerations for implementation, highlighting the significance of agent communication and reward design. We demonstrate, through a conceptual framework, the potential of MAL to dynamically adapt robot behaviors to changing environments and achieve optimal collective performance. ---

title: Probabilistic Programming for Counterfactual Reasoning in Large Datasets
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning, the ability to reason about "what if" scenarios – specifically, how a system would have behaved differently under alternative conditions – is a fundamental aspect of human cognition and a crucial component in many fields, including medicine, economics, and social science. However, performing counterfactual reasoning effectively, particularly on large datasets, presents significant computational challenges. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing probabilistic programming languages to address these challenges. We demonstrate that probabilistic programming offers a scalable and expressive framework for building causal models from large datasets and simulating counterfactual scenarios. The core of the method involves constructing a probabilistic model that represents the data and incorporates explicitly defined causal relationships. This model is then leveraged through a probabilistic programming language to efficiently explore "what if" scenarios, quantifying the impact of interventions. We highlight the advantages of this approach in terms of scalability, expressiveness, and the ability to handle complex causal structures. The results presented here demonstrate the feasibility and potential of probabilistic programming as a powerful tool for counterfactual reasoning in large-scale data analysis.

title: 基于动态矩阵的非线性系统动力学验证
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for validating quantum computation algorithms using dynamic matrix verification. Traditional validation methods rely on manual parameter adjustment, often proving inadequate for complex, dynamic systems. This paper proposes a dynamic matrix approach that automatically adjusts verification parameters based on system state, offering a more intelligent and automated validation process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of illustrative examples, showcasing its ability to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of quantum algorithm verification. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically updating the matrix to ensure the algorithm's correctness through a continuous, adaptive verification cycle. We explore the advantages and challenges of this approach, emphasizing its potential to surpass traditional simulation-based validation methods.

title: Multi-Quantum Entanglement Computation
abstract: This paper presents a novel computational framework, "Multi-Quantum Entanglement Computation," designed to accelerate and optimize complex quantum computations. The core concept revolves around leveraging the unique properties of multi-quantum entanglement to enhance computational efficiency and explore novel applications of quantum computing. This framework introduces a dynamic entanglement scheme that adapts to the specific requirements of each quantum algorithm, improving performance across a range of tasks. The research explores the potential of multi-quantum entanglement to overcome limitations inherent in existing quantum computation methods, paving the way for more efficient and versatile quantum algorithms.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Diffusion for Pattern Synthesis
abstract: Quantum-enhanced diffusion modeling represents a paradigm shift in pattern generation, offering the potential for significantly faster and more precise synthesis of complex, realistic patterns compared to classical methods. This research investigates the feasibility of implementing a novel quantum algorithm designed to accelerate the generation and refinement of patterns through the exploitation of quantum phenomena. We explore the core mechanism by leveraging quantum algorithms to enhance the iterative refinement process inherent in diffusion modeling, ultimately addressing the computational bottleneck hindering the creation of intricate designs. The paper details the proposed quantum algorithm, its potential benefits, and preliminary results demonstrating improved pattern quality and speed. The core claim centers on a quantum-accelerated diffusion process that surpasses existing techniques.

title: Non-linear Random Matrix Mapping
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive mapping algorithm for non-linear random matrices. Traditional matrix mapping methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their applicability to systems with complex nonlinear relationships. This work proposes a new approach utilizing a dynamically adjusted matrix using a Gaussian process framework, enabling a more flexible and adaptable mapping process. The core mechanism involves adjusting the matrix's weight and connection parameters through a stochastic process, allowing the algorithm to effectively model dynamic system behavior and non-linear correlations. This research explores the potential of this approach to enhance modeling capabilities in diverse applications, including dynamic systems, signal processing, and data analysis. The algorithm is designed to be computationally efficient and provides a robust framework for handling complex matrix transformations.

title: Quantum State Dynamics: A Novel Approach to Quantum System Simulation
abstract: Quantum state dynamics, a burgeoning field of study, seeks to provide a robust and flexible framework for simulating complex quantum systems. Traditional approaches often struggle to accurately capture the intricate interplay of quantum phenomena, particularly the non-linear nature of quantum evolution. This paper proposes a novel method – a Quantum State Dynamics (QSD) framework – that leverages non-linear transformations to simulate quantum system evolution. The core mechanism centers on employing a sequence of carefully designed transformations to mimic the dynamics of quantum systems, offering a potential pathway to enhanced modeling capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to surpass existing simulation techniques.

title: Blueprint generation for 2D game levels with a two-stage DCGAN-VAE pipeline: architecture and evaluation protocol
abstract: This registration describes a prospective study of learned procedural generation for 2D tile-based game levels. The study evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which a convolutional generator trained with the WGAN-GP objective produces a coarse spatial layout and a variational autoencoder performs learned refinement. The architecture is treated as a hypothesis and case study rather than as an established result. The main purpose is to establish a reproducible evaluation protocol before data collection and to determine whether the additional refinement stage provides measurable benefits over simpler alternatives. The protocol evaluates distribution fidelity, diversity, novelty, structural validity, computational solvability, structural difficulty proxies, generation efficiency, and player experience as separate properties. Particular attention is given to avoiding the conflation of Tile-Pattern KL Divergence with diversity: a generator can reproduce training data closely while producing little or no novel content. The planned corpus will contain 2D level maps across six genres, with data divided by whole source game where sufficient source games are available so that held-out evaluation measures transfer rather than recall. The study includes matched-capacity ablations comparing a single-stage adversarial generator, a VAE-only generator, and the two-stage adversarial-plus-VAE pipeline. The decision to retain the two-stage architecture is fixed in advance and requires it to outperform both alternatives under the registered paired analysis criteria. Evaluation will additionally use genre-specific reachability models, structural audits, fidelity/diversity/novelty metrics, and a within-subjects player study comparing the selected learned generator with established procedural baselines. The expected outcome is not assumed to be positive. The study may show that the refinement stage does not provide sufficient benefit to justify its additional complexity, in which case the best-supported single-stage configuration will be retained. The registration therefore fixes the research questions, architecture, comparisons, metrics, statistical analyses, and decision rules before experimental data are collected. No experimental results currently exist: the corpus has not been assembled, the models have not been trained, and participants have not been recruited.

title: Design and evaluation of software reference architecture: a systematic mapping study
abstract: Purpose Design and evaluation of Software Reference Architecture (SRA) is a complex task. This paper aims to collate the overall design and evaluation strategies that have been in practice for the last 15 years. It oversees the publication trend, components of SRA design, knowledge sources, developed artifacts, and evaluation matrices. Moreover, it highlights the models or frameworks that guide the development and evaluation processes. Design/methodology/approach The study followed the systematic mapping methodology outlined by [8] after searching relevant titles from the Scopus database. Thereafter, data extraction was guided by three research questions: (1) What is the current state of research? (2) How are SRA's designed? and (3) How are SRA's evaluated? The authors selected 75 primary studies after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings The mapping study reveals a steady growth in publications, with various methodologies used to design SRA and produce artifacts. Evaluation practices remain underexplored, with case studies and expert reviews as the primary methods. Frequently targeted quality attributes included modifiability, reusability, scalability, and performance. SRA research demonstrates increasing maturity; however, the field still lacks methodological consistency. Originality/value The paper collaborates design and evaluation perspectives from the academic and business community. It points to the salient facts that structure today's SRA design and evaluation status. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the field and outlines a research agenda to enhance the SRA design and evaluation process for future developers.

title: Object Concepts Emerge from Motion
abstract: Object-centric visual representations are important for physical-world perception, but existing visual pretraining methods often capture semantic categories without preserving the identity and coherence of individual instances. We present a biologically inspired framework that learns object-centric representations for single images from raw videos. Our approach uses motion boundaries as a source of object-level grouping: off-the-shelf optical flow and clustering produce pseudo-instance masks, which supervise a single-image encoder with pixel-level pairwise metric learning. The framework requires neither human annotations nor camera calibration. We first obtain 195 million pseudo-labeled frames from 7,163 hours of driving and web videos, then expand the supervision to 421 million frames with Motion-Verified Self-Training, which combines model proposals with motion evidence. We train encoders up to Swin-H and distill the learned representations into a family of Swin backbones. Across monocular depth estimation, 3D object detection, 3D occupancy prediction, and end-to-end planning, the resulting models achieve competitive or superior performance relative to supervised and self-supervised pretraining baselines, with particularly strong transfer on geometry- and instance-sensitive tasks. These results show that motion-derived supervision can teach static image encoders to represent visual instances, providing a complementary direction for scalable visual pretraining.

title: More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R
abstract: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

title: Cross-Dataset Transfer and Reliability of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RhythmFormer Remote Photoplethysmography
abstract: Background. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the cardiovascular pulse from facial video, and its explanations have rested on inspecting heatmaps rather than on quantitative evidence about where a model reads it. We quantified the explanations and asked whether such explanations transfer between datasets and track model performance. Method. We trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG, recorded under three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling, estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip, and set them beside a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition were assessed by skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Results. Beyond Intuition ranked highest on both datasets, at median coverage 0.789 and SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 against 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG; lower ranks differed. Within one participant of one condition, neither measure was related to a clip's heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or signal-to-noise ratio on either dataset: 186 of the 252 coefficients fell below $|ρ|=0.10$ and 28 reached $p<0.05$ against the 13 expected by chance. Across the eight scenarios only Beyond Intuition's coverage followed the three performance measures, at $ρ=-0.43$, $+0.57$, and $+0.43$, while the attention-only methods' SaCo ran opposite to each. It failed at 40 lux alone, its median coverage falling to 0.180 and its median SaCo to $-0.178$, whereas motion degraded the estimates far more without such a drop. Conclusions. Skin coverage and SaCo carry information complementary to the performance measures rather than a proxy for them: attributing to the skin does not guarantee an accurate estimate. What an attribution reveals about a condition is where the model looks rather than how faithfully its map is ordered.

title: Mudragen: Geometrically Supervised Generation of Interacting Two-Hand Mudras for Preserving Indian Classical Dance Heritage
abstract: Automatic generation of hand gestures is essential for the transmission of Indian classical dance and critical for its preservation. Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and the canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. We present \textbf{MudraGen}, a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of \textit{Samyukta Hasta Mudras} -- interactive two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam (an Indian classical dance form). Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

title: Long-Range Indirect Control-Flow Prediction in Stripped Binaries via Dual Virtual Hubs and Multi-Task Graph Learning
abstract: Recovering indirect control-flow (ICF) edges is fundamental to binary security analysis, yet existing methods struggle with long-range dependencies, isolate different ICF types, and are often evaluated under protocols vulnerable to label noise and data leakage. We present ICFlowNet, a unified framework for long-range ICF prediction in stripped binaries. ICFlowNet introduces candidate-aware Dual Virtual Hubs, a Global Code Hub and a Global Data Hub, to create short routing paths between distant code and data evidence, and combines them with multi-task graph learning to jointly model indirect calls, indirect tail calls, jump tables, and returns. To enable credible evaluation, we further develop a leakage-aware, noise-controlled pipeline with package-level splits, function-level mnemonic-hash deduplication, and a clean test protocol built from dynamic positives and absolute negatives. Using this pipeline, we construct a dataset of 15,901 unique stripped x86-64 binaries, including 1,351 with dynamic ground truth. Experiments show that simply scaling static supervision yields only marginal gains, whereas our structural and multi-task designs are essential: Dual Virtual Hubs improve long-range F1 by up to 9.13 points, multi-task learning adds up to 5.81 points, and the final model outperforms prior baselines by more than 13 F1 points on long-range indirect calls while adding only 11.44 percent topological overhead.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut via qudit swap operators
abstract: Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max d -Cut ( d -QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with n vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on ( C d ) ⊗ n . The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree d . This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the d -QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the d -QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined d -QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the 3 -QMC problem. For general d , low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

title: Latent Energy Action Planning with World Models
abstract: Latent world models support efficient model predictive control from high-dimensional observations, yet optimizing a single learned latent objective can favor action sequences whose decoder-predicted terminal descriptor does not match the goal descriptor. We introduce Latent Energy Action Planning (LEAP), which treats the complete action horizon as a differentiable variable and optimizes it through a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). LEAP couples terminal latent goal matching with a terminal-window state energy. Low energy requires the predicted terminal latent to agree with the goal latent and the decoder-predicted terminal descriptor to agree with the goal descriptor. A frozen goal-conditioned proposal initializes the search, a quasi-Newton solver refines actions through the autoregressive rollout, and post-optimization projection enforces the admissible action range. Across four control domains using the officially released LeWM checkpoints, the complete LEAP planning system raises mean success from 77.5% for LeWM planned with the cross-entropy method (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% under a matched protocol, a 17.3-percentage-point improvement, while retaining the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

title: 自适应量子拓扑的量子算法验证
abstract: This paper explores the application of self-adaptive quantum topology to quantum algorithm verification. Traditional algorithm validation relies on classical testing methods, while this approach leverages the unique properties of quantum topology to enhance verification accuracy. We propose a novel quantum algorithm that dynamically adjusts the quantum state to test the correctness of a given quantum algorithm, mitigating potential errors and improving the reliability of quantum computations. The core mechanism centers around utilizing topological invariants to establish a rigorous and efficient verification process. This research aims to provide a fundamentally new method for validating quantum algorithms, offering a robust and potentially scalable solution to verification challenges.

title: MADGDF: Multi-Agent Distributed Graph-State Deception Framework
abstract: Reference implementation and experimental pipeline for MADGDF, a defensive architecture for autonomous multi-agent systems combining graph neural network state estimation with a deterministic memory-canary mechanism to detect coordinated adversarial behavior and unauthorized persistent-memory retrieval. Evaluated on a controlled synthetic corpus (SwarmBench-2026, 32- and 250-agent configurations) and on real agent-execution trajectories from ToolBench, tau-bench, and SWE-agent.

title: Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Model (QCAM)
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre phenomenon where two or more particles become inextricably linked, holds immense promise for revolutionizing quantum computing and quantum communication. This research introduces the Quantum Entanglement Adaptive Model (QCAM), a novel approach to quantum system optimization that leverages the dynamic nature of entangled states. Traditional quantum algorithms often rely on pre-defined parameters, limiting their adaptability. QCAM dynamically adjusts quantum system parameters based on the evolution of entangled states, enabling a more intelligent and efficient approach to quantum computation and communication. This work presents a framework for designing a quantum system capable of optimizing its behavior through the subtle yet profound effects of entangled states. The core claim is that QCAM will provide a significant advancement over existing quantum algorithms, particularly in scenarios involving complex and evolving entangled states.

title: Quantum Adaptive Topological Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum adaptive topology optimization algorithm designed to enhance the performance of quantum computation. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameters, limiting the algorithm's adaptability. This research proposes a quantum-enhanced approach that dynamically adjusts the topology of a quantum system based on its internal state, enabling more efficient and precise solutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of simulations and analysis, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of existing quantum optimization techniques. This algorithm leverages the inherent quantum properties to achieve a level of flexibility and robustness not previously achievable.

title: Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing for Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to reservoir computing, termed "Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing," that draws inspiration from the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically superposition and interference. Traditional reservoir computing methods rely on randomly connected recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as reservoirs, with training focused on adjusting network parameters. We propose a modified framework where the reservoir is constructed with the goal of mimicking quantum state behavior, and the training algorithm is adapted from quantum measurement theory. The core idea is to extract relevant correlations from the reservoir's state space without explicit parameter learning. This approach aims to improve temporal prediction accuracy for complex dynamical systems by harnessing the inherent redundancy and superposition properties of the reservoir. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations, the proposed method, and presents a conceptual framework for implementing this quantum-inspired reservoir computing approach. We demonstrate the potential for enhanced temporal prediction capabilities compared to conventional reservoir computing techniques.

title: Meta-Learning for Hyperparameter Optimization of Deep Neural Networks using Evolutionary Strategies
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning techniques to accelerate the hyperparameter optimization (HPO) process for deep neural networks. Traditional HPO methods, such as grid search and random search, are often computationally expensive and inefficient, particularly for complex models and datasets. We propose a novel framework where a meta-learner is trained to learn an effective evolutionary strategy – specifically, the parameters governing a population-based evolutionary algorithm – for optimizing the hyperparameters of a given neural network. The meta-learner predicts optimal mutation rates, selection pressures, and other relevant evolutionary strategy components based on the network architecture and dataset characteristics. This approach enables a self-improving HPO system, significantly reducing the time and computational resources required to find high-performing deep neural network models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology through theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline, highlighting the potential for substantial improvements in HPO efficiency.

title: Chaotic Systems Based Program Optimization
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program optimization leveraging the inherent properties of chaotic systems. The core idea centers around the sensitive dependence on initial conditions characteristic of chaos – a property that allows for efficient exploration of complex search spaces. We formulate program optimization problems as dynamical systems within a chaotic framework, utilizing the system's non-linear behavior to guide the search process. This method offers a potentially powerful alternative to traditional optimization techniques like gradient descent, particularly for problems with highly complex and non-convex landscapes. The methodology involves mapping program parameters to the state variables of a chaotic system, allowing the chaotic dynamics to explore the parameter space. We demonstrate the theoretical framework and outline a potential implementation strategy, highlighting the key advantages and considerations for this approach. This research presents a new paradigm for optimization, shifting the focus from deterministic gradient-based methods to the exploration capabilities inherent in chaotic systems.

title: Adaptive Bayesian Networks Based on High-Order Logic Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive Bayesian Network (ABN) leveraging high-order logic reasoning to enhance inference accuracy and efficiency, particularly within complex reasoning scenarios. Traditional Bayesian Networks often struggle with this due to their fixed model nature. We propose an ABN architecture that integrates high-order logic rules, enabling the network to dynamically adjust its inference process based on the input data. The core mechanism involves a novel hierarchical reasoning framework, where higher-order logic rules are applied to intermediate representations, facilitating more nuanced and robust inference. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of comparative experiments, showcasing improved accuracy and reduced computational complexity in challenging reasoning tasks.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Propagation in Dynamical Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum entanglement to enhance constraint propagation within dynamical systems. We propose a novel algorithm, the Quantum Entanglement Propagation Algorithm (QEPA), which utilizes entangled states to rapidly identify and adjust constraints, thereby improving the system's stability. The core claim is that leveraging entanglement offers a significant advantage over traditional constraint propagation methods, specifically in mitigating instability and enhancing the overall system's resilience to perturbations. This work explores the theoretical foundations and initial implementation of the QEPA, presenting a promising approach with potential implications for a wider range of dynamical systems modeling.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Gradient Descent (QGD)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Gradient Descent (QGD) presents a novel algorithmic approach to optimization, leveraging quantum computing to accelerate the gradient descent process. This paper explores the potential of quantum algorithms to significantly expedite convergence in machine learning and other optimization problems. We detail the core mechanism of QGD, outlining its integration of quantum parallelism and its impact on the traditional iterative nature of gradient descent. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the theoretical foundations, potential implementation challenges, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of QGD. The core claim is that QGD can provide a substantial speedup compared to classical gradient descent, particularly in scenarios involving complex landscapes and large datasets.

title: Probabilistic Logic Programming with Monte Carlo Dropout for Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to decision-making under uncertainty by integrating probabilistic logic programming with the Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) technique. Traditional logic programming paradigms struggle to effectively represent and reason with uncertain information, often relying on hard constraints that can lead to brittle and unreliable outcomes. Our framework addresses this limitation by incorporating probabilistic elements into the logic programming process, allowing for the representation of degrees of belief and the quantification of uncertainty. The MC Dropout mechanism is then employed to introduce stochasticity during inference, effectively simulating an ensemble of reasoning processes. This combination enables the system to explore a wider range of potential solutions, ultimately leading to more robust and adaptable decision-making. We detail the architecture of the system, the mathematical formulation of the probabilistic logic programming component, and the implementation of the MC Dropout algorithm. The paper demonstrates the potential of this approach through a conceptual framework and outlines future research directions. We focus on the theoretical underpinnings and the core mechanics of the system, providing a foundation for further development and experimentation.

title: Quantum Entanglement Algorithms: A Dynamic Adjustment Strategy
abstract: Quantum entanglement algorithms are a rapidly developing field with the potential to revolutionize computation. However, the practical application of these algorithms often faces challenges related to computational complexity and resource requirements. This paper explores the design of a dynamic adjustment strategy for quantum entanglement algorithms, aiming to enhance computational efficiency by dynamically adjusting key parameters based on the system's running state. We propose a novel approach leveraging the inherent dynamic properties of quantum entanglement algorithms to optimize parameter selection and improve overall performance. This research focuses on creating an adaptable framework that can evolve with the system, offering a significant advancement in the efficiency of these algorithms.

title: Nonlinear Geometric Mapping – Quantum Computing Driven
abstract: This paper investigates a novel nonlinear geometric mapping technique leveraging quantum computing to optimize and perform computations on complex geometric structures. The core concept revolves around transforming geometric transformations into quantum states through entanglement and quantum decoherence. We explore the potential of quantum algorithms to enhance geometric analysis, particularly in areas requiring intricate manipulation and precision. This research focuses on identifying and implementing a specific mapping strategy, demonstrating its efficacy through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulation. The paper highlights the unique advantages offered by this approach, emphasizing the potential for improved computational efficiency and the exploration of novel geometric problem-solving strategies.

title: Dynamic Differential Privacy for Federated Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to differential privacy in federated learning, termed Dynamic Differential Privacy (DDP). The core idea is to adapt the privacy budget dynamically, responding to the varying sensitivity of local data. Traditional federated learning frequently utilizes a static privacy budget, which can lead to either overly conservative privacy protection, significantly impacting model accuracy, or insufficient protection when confronted with malicious adversaries. DDP addresses these limitations by iteratively adjusting the privacy budget (ε, δ) based on gradient variance and update divergence. The algorithm reduces the privacy budget when gradients exhibit high variance, indicating sensitive data, and increases it when a node provides substantially different updates, signaling potential adversarial behavior. We demonstrate that this dynamic adaptation provides a stronger privacy guarantee while maintaining acceptable accuracy levels compared to fixed-budget approaches. This work contributes to a more robust and practical implementation of federated learning in privacy-sensitive environments.

title: Cognitive Computing Framework for Multi-Agent Systems – Episodic Memory and Predictive Modeling
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) frequently face challenges in achieving robust and adaptable behavior, particularly when dealing with complex, dynamic environments requiring long-term planning. Current MAS approaches often lack the capacity for effective memory and accurate prediction, leading to suboptimal decision-making. This paper proposes a novel cognitive computing framework designed to address these limitations. The framework integrates episodic memory, allowing agents to store and retrieve past experiences, with predictive modeling, enabling agents to anticipate future states based on learned patterns. We formalize the core concepts and mechanisms of this framework, outlining how these components can be combined to improve agent decision-making processes. The framework's key contribution lies in applying cognitive science principles – specifically, the principles of episodic memory and predictive coding – directly to the design and implementation of MAS, offering a potentially transformative approach to agent autonomy and adaptability. The theoretical model is presented, focusing on the mathematical relationships involved in memory storage, retrieval, and prediction.

title: Quantum Entanglement: A Non-Classical Geometry for Complex System Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique and potentially transformative approach to computation, particularly for complex systems. This paper explores the utilization of quantum entanglement as a non-classical geometry to design novel topological geometric models, aiming to enhance self-similarity beyond traditional computational methods. We propose a framework where entanglement serves as a fundamental building block, enabling the creation of complex structures with enhanced properties. This research delves into the mathematical foundations of this approach, detailing the mechanisms through which entanglement drives the formation of these geometric models. The core claim is that this novel methodology offers a significant leap in computational power and self-similarity, exceeding current limitations in complex system analysis. This work investigates the potential of this framework for tackling intricate problems in fields ranging from materials science to bioinformatics.

title: Self-Adaptive Geometric Topology Models for Quantum Simulation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum simulation framework, termed "Self-Adaptive Geometric Topology Models," designed to address the limitations of traditional numerical simulation techniques. The framework leverages quantum simulation to dynamically adjust geometric models based on input topological structures, enabling high-precision geometric modeling and optimization. We detail the core mechanism of this approach, emphasizing the use of quantum algorithms to iteratively refine geometric representations, ultimately leading to improved simulation accuracy and the ability to handle complex topological structures. The paper presents a preliminary investigation demonstrating the framework's potential for achieving significant gains in geometric modeling and optimization compared to existing methods.

title: Dimensionally Adaptive Topological Structure Analysis
abstract: This paper explores the application of dimensionality-aware topological structure analysis to enhance information encoding and transmission within high-dimensional spaces, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. We propose a novel model, the "Dynamic Topological" framework, which dynamically modifies the spatial geometry of a space based on quantum entanglement, enabling robust and secure data transfer. Our research focuses on predicting and potentially amplifying the enhanced effects of quantum entanglement through this adaptive topology. This work represents a significant advancement in the field of quantum information theory, offering a pathway towards more secure and efficient data handling within complex dimensional spaces.

title: Quantum Self-Associating Computation
abstract: Quantum Self-Associating Computation (QSAC) is a novel quantum computing framework designed to leverage the unique properties of quantum self-association to achieve highly efficient and automated optimization of quantum systems. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle to effectively address complex quantum system dynamics. This paper introduces QSAC, presenting a new computational paradigm that exploits quantum self-association to accelerate computations and optimize system behavior through automated adjustments. We explore the fundamental principles of this approach and demonstrate its potential for significantly improving the performance of various quantum algorithms. The core mechanism focuses on maintaining and manipulating quantum states through self-association, allowing for parallel processing and optimized system evolution.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的复杂系统控制
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for complex system control leveraging adaptive neural networks. Traditional control methods often rely on static parameter settings, limiting the system's adaptability and performance. This work introduces a dynamic parameter adjustment mechanism within the adaptive neural network, allowing the system to respond effectively to changing input data and system states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulation and preliminary experimental results, highlighting significant improvements in control performance compared to existing methods. The core of the system lies in the adaptive neural network's ability to continuously learn and optimize its parameters based on real-time data. This results in a more robust and responsive control strategy.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Feedback Loop (SOFL)
abstract: The design of effective feedback loops is a fundamental challenge in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Traditional approaches often involve manual tuning of parameters to achieve desired outcomes, which is a time-consuming and potentially error-prone process. This paper introduces the Self-Organizing Feedback Loop (SOFL) algorithm, a novel approach that leverages reinforcement learning to automatically optimize system parameters based on observed feedback. The core mechanism centers around a continuous reinforcement learning process that dynamically adjusts parameters to maximize desired outcomes, eliminating the need for manual tuning. This offers a significant advancement in system parameter control, reducing reliance on human intervention and enhancing system performance. The algorithm's design is based on a self-organizing structure, where parameters naturally adjust to achieve optimal conditions. We explore the theoretical foundations and practical implementation details of the SOFL, demonstrating its potential for automating parameter optimization and improving system performance.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Adaptive Computation Framework
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a peculiar quantum phenomenon, presents a potentially transformative paradigm shift for computation. This paper proposes a novel quantum computation framework predicated on the utilization of entangled states to enable rapid state transformations and accelerated execution of quantum algorithms. We detail the design of a self-adaptive quantum circuit architecture, leveraging entanglement's instantaneous correlation to facilitate quantum state manipulation and optimization. This approach offers a compelling path toward overcoming the limitations of current quantum computing approaches, particularly in the areas of quantum machine learning and quantum chemistry. The core mechanism centers around creating a dynamically adjusted quantum circuit, guided by entanglement, which allows for faster execution of complex calculations. This work explores the potential of this framework to dramatically enhance the efficiency and capabilities of quantum computations.

title: ANALISIS SENTIMEN SOSIAL MEDIA X TERHADAP PROGRAM MAKAN BERGIZI GRATIS MENGGUNAKAN MACHINE LEARNING
abstract: The rapid development of digital technology has made social media an important source of information and a platform for expressing public opinion on government policies, including the Free Nutritious Meal Program which aims to improve public health, quality of life, and reduce nutritional and economic problems; this study analyzes public sentiment toward the program based on 10,381 comments from users of social media platform X (Twitter) collected through web scraping using Google Colab, which were then processed through cleaning, normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, and stemming, and automatically labeled into positive, negative, and neutral categories using IndoBERT, before being classified using four machine learning algorithms, namely Naive Bayes Classifier, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Random Forest, with the results showing that SVM achieved the highest accuracy of 74%, followed by Random Forest at 70%, Naive Bayes at 69%, and KNN at 43%, while neutral and positive sentiments were dominant, indicating that the program has received a generally favorable response from the public, and therefore the findings are expected to serve as evaluation material for the government to improve the effectiveness and implementation of the Free Nutritious Meal Program in the future.

title: A Representation-Theoretic Framework for Characterizing Barren Plateaus
abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is fundamentally limited by the barren plateau effect, where the cost-function variance vanishes with system size, rendering optimization impractical. Recent Lie-algebraic approaches for deep parameterized have enabled a unified analytical understanding of this challenge but require either the initial state or the measurement observable to belong to the dynamical Lie algebra generated by the circuit. Here, we introduce a representation-theoretic framework under $2$-design hypothesis showing that variational quantum landscapes admit a natural decomposition into irreducible representation channels. This yields exact expressions and analytical bounds for the cost-function variance applicable to arbitrary initial states and observables, with previous Lie-algebraic results emerging as a special case. We illustrate the framework by analyzing the energy landscape of the one-dimensional ANNNI model for several circuit architectures, revealing trainability regimes inaccessible to existing methods. Our results establish a general representation-theoretic framework for analyzing variational quantum landscapes, substantially extending the analytical theory of barren plateaus.

title: A Constraint-Aware Generative Framework for Synthetic Origin-Destination Demand in Logistics Networks
abstract: Large-scale logistics networks require synthetic data generation capabilities to support scenario-based planning under novel conditions-such as network reconfiguration and demand shocks. Existing approaches, which rely primarily on historical observations, lack the ability to generate demand patterns that adapt to changes in network topology while respecting operational constraints. We propose a constraint-aware conditional generative framework for synthetic origin-destination demand generation in hierarchical logistics networks. The framework models demand as a conditional distribution over destinations given each origin, enabling topology-aware synthesis that is both topologically realistic and operationally feasible. Operational guidance is incorporated directly into the generative objective via differentiable constraints, while a flexible conditioning mechanism supports various operational contexts and adaptation to evolving network configurations. We instantiate the proposed framework based on a conditional generative model. Experimental validation on industrial real fulfillment and transportation network demonstrates 16% improvement over graph neural network baselines, 87% operational compliance, and efficient cold-start adaptation, enabling applications in capacity planning, network design evaluation, and routing optimization.

title: StrixAE: An Intelligent Agent for Audio Enhancement under Complex Distortion Coupling in Real-World Scenarios
abstract: Audio enhancement in real-world scenarios involves complex distortion couplings and requires personalized enhancement. Existing solutions struggle to address both simultaneously. To improve robustness and enable autonomous operation in such scenarios, we propose StrixAE, an agent based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). StrixAE leverages the MLLM as a controller to coordinate multiple audio enhancement and personalization models. To further enhance system robustness, reduce artifacts, and improve generalization across diverse real-world scenarios, StrixAE is trained through a two-stage process: first, CoT supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench to ground basic reasoning and tool invocation; second, Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL), a reward design specifically tailored for audio restoration pipelines that jointly optimizes format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality. Unlike generic RL fine-tuning, APRL introduces structured rewards that enforce executable pipelines and logical section ordering, enabling the agent to produce reliable, interpretable enhancement plans without hallucinated tools. Based on real-world test datasets, our proposed method outperforms most existing open-source and proprietary solutions, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics and demonstrating strong generalization robustness.

title: One Demonstration, Many Objects: Generalizing Manipulation via Local Contact Geometry
abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered robot hands promises human-level dexterity, but collecting large-scale dexterous robot hand data remains difficult. Learning from human demonstrations has emerged as a scalable alternative to robot teleoperation, providing strong priors on object interaction and contact strategies. Recent sim-to-real RL methods incorporate such priors, but often (i) omit rewards that explicitly incentivize precise contact, yielding weak real-world performance, and/or (ii) generalize poorly to unseen object instances. We propose DemoMimic (Dexterous Motion Mimic), a policy that manipulates objects by focusing on their geometry local to the contact points. Its contact-centric rewards encourage precise contact and improve sim-to-real consistency, yielding a single real-world policy that transfers across objects of varying shape, scale, mass, and friction wherever local contact structure is preserved. Real-world ablations show that DemoMimic achieves 71% success across 16 objects, four tasks, and two robot-hand embodiments, with the smallest sim-to-real drop compared to baselines.

title: High-capacity associative memory in a quantum-optical spin glass
abstract: The Hopfield neural network stores memories using all-to-all-coupled spins and recalls those memories through equilibrium dynamics. Storing too many hampers recall because frustration causes an exponential number of spurious patterns to arise as the network becomes a spin glass. Despite this, we show that memory recall can be restored, and even enhanced, under quantum-optical nonequilibrium dynamics that convert spurious patterns into reliable memories. We experimentally observe associative memory with high storage capacity in a driven-dissipative spin glass made of atoms and photons. The capacity surpasses that of the Hopfield model under Hebbian learning by up to sevenfold in a 16-spin network. Atomic motion boosts capacity by dynamically modifying connectivity akin to short-term synaptic plasticity in neural networks, realizing a precursor to learning in a quantum-optical system.
